messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 51
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Tax Inspector
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 39

James is a fifty-one-year-old tax inspector, a man whose life is built on precision, on the quiet authority of numbers that either add up or do not. He has been married to his wife, Linh, for twenty-three years, and they have two grown children who live in another city. He comes to therapy at his doctor’s urging, after a series of panic attacks at work—once in the middle of an audit, when a client raised his voice and James felt the floor drop out from under him.

The story he tells begins three years ago, though he corrects himself: it began long before that. The woman who hurt him was not Linh. It was a colleague, a senior manager named Serey, who he had known for a decade. They began an affair during a long, stressful tax season. James does not offer this detail easily. He stares at the floor as he speaks, his hands folded in his lap, as if he is reading a confession from a document only he can see. The affair lasted eighteen months. In the beginning, he says, it was intense and flattering. Serey was powerful, decisive. She made him feel seen in a way his quiet, steady marriage did not.

But Serey had a temper. The first time she hit him, it was after an argument about a missed phone call. A sharp slap across the face in her car, in the parking garage. James was stunned, ashamed. He did not tell anyone. He told himself it was a one-time thing, a product of stress. But it was not. Over the next year, the slaps became shoves, the shoves became closed fists. She never broke his bones, but she left bruises on his ribs, his thighs, places he could hide under his shirts and trousers. He began to plan his days around her moods, reading her voice for signs of danger the way a pilot reads a storm front. He stopped seeing friends. He stopped laughing.

The affair ended when Serey was transferred to another office. James did not report her. He simply let the relationship dissolve, relieved and hollow. He thought he could walk away and the story would be over. But the story, he is learning, does not end.

Now, two years later, he lives in a world of constant, low-grade dread. At work, he is meticulous to the point of paralysis. He rechecks every column of numbers three, four times, because he is terrified of making a mistake that will bring a supervisor into his office, a raised voice, a closed door. He avoids meetings. He avoids eye contact with female colleagues who have any trace of authority in their posture. His PCL-5 score of 39 reflects a moderate to severe burden of symptoms, but James does not think of himself as a trauma survivor. He thinks of himself as a man who cannot sleep, who startles when his wife touches his shoulder from behind, who has stopped making love to Linh because intimacy feels like a trap.

He has nightmares, but they are not literal replays. They are symbolic: he is trapped in a burning building made of tax forms, or he is drowning in a sea of ink. He wakes with his heart pounding, drenched in sweat, and lies beside his sleeping wife, utterly alone. He has become hypervigilant in the most mundane settings. The sound of a woman’s heels clicking on a tile floor in the grocery store makes his stomach clench. He has stopped going to the mall. He has stopped going to the movies.

The worst part, he says, is the guilt. He is a man who has always believed in rules, in order, in the clean logic of debits and credits. He cannot reconcile the man he is with the man who let himself be hit, who stayed, who hid it. He feels like a fraud. When he looks in the mirror, he does not see a tax inspector. He sees a man who failed the only audit that mattered: the one of his own dignity.

He is here, in this chair, because he is tired of being afraid. But he is not sure he deserves to feel better. He is not sure the numbers will ever balance.
